category: Cave diving — fatal accident / body recovery
working_title: He Went 270 m Down to Bring a Body Home
alt_title: The Promise That Killed Dave Shaw
subject: Boesmansgat (Bushman's Hole), Northern Cape, South Africa. Oct 2004: Dave Shaw found the body of Deon Dreyer (died Dec 1994) at ~270 m (Wikipedia gives 272 m). 8 Jan 2005: Shaw died trying to recover it. Support diver Don Shirley went down to ~250 m to look for him, got decompression sickness and was left with permanent balance damage. On 12 Jan 2005, while Shaw's equipment was being recovered, both bodies floated up close to the surface and were recovered.
why_potential: Combines the niche's two strongest triggers: body recovery (Dive Talk 9.15M) and an extreme number (270 m, ~15-min descent vs ~12-h ascent). Covered repeatedly in long-form (MrBallen, doc 'Dave Not Coming Back') and in Shorts, including non-English ones, so demand travels. Few 3D-animated Shorts exist. A depth cross-section is ideal for our pipeline.

working_title: 13 Trapped Behind Kilometres of Flooded Cave
alt_title: The Rescue That Shouldn't Have Worked
subject: Tham Luang Nang Non, Chiang Rai, Thailand. 23 June 2018: 12 boys of the Wild Boars football team and their coach were trapped by monsoon flooding. British divers Rick Stanton and John Volanthen found them alive on 2 July. All 13 were brought out through flooded passages 8–10 July. Former Thai Navy SEAL Saman Kunan died on 6 July.
why_potential: Highest raw demand signal in the set: Zack D. Films' 3D Short was reported at ~60M views (unverified). It's a rescue with hope, so it's advertiser-safe and has a broad audience. Risk: heavily covered, so we need a fresh angle (one specific moment: the 'how many of you?' discovery or the sedated dive out).

working_title: Under the Ice, the Only Way Out Was Deeper
alt_title: Five Divers Went In. Three Came Out.
subject: Plura / Steinugleflåget cave system, Plurdalen, Rana, Norway. 6 Feb 2014: five Finnish divers (Patrik Grönqvist, Jari Huotarinen, Vesa Rantanen, Jari Uusimäki, Kai Känkänen) attempted a traverse entering through a hole cut in river ice. Huotarinen died shortly after the deepest section (~110 m below the entrance level). Uusimäki also died; police believe he panicked on finding Huotarinen, while Känkänen tried to help him (reported). The three survivors exited after long decompression.
why_potential: Ice entry, a deep traverse with no easy way back, and a survivor forced to pass a body make a vivid story. Multiple long-form and Short versions exist, plus a feature documentary (2016). Plura's dive centre has complained that YouTube is full of misleading Plura videos (divers24.com), so an accurate, careful version can stand out.

working_title: Stuck Upside Down With No Way to Back Out
alt_title: The Cave They Sealed With Him Inside
subject: Nutty Putty Cave, Utah, USA. 24 Nov 2009 (one source says 25 Nov): John Edward Jones, a 26-year-old medical student, became stuck head-down in an ~18x10-inch crevice about 700 ft into the cave. Rescuers partly freed him, but a rope-and-pulley system failed (NBC: a roof anchor gave way) and he slipped back. He died around 12:30 a.m. after ~27–28 hours. The cave was sealed with his body inside.
why_potential: Biggest proven entrapment demand (FatalBreakdown 13.09M; Zack D. Films also animated it). It is dry caving, but the audience overlaps fully. Included as 1 of 2 allowed adjacent stories. Risk: very saturated, so our angle must be the rescue mechanics (the pulley that failed) rather than a straight retelling.

working_title: 60 Hours in an Air Bubble Under Mallorca
alt_title: He Survived by Breathing the Cave
subject: Sa Piqueta cave (Cova de sa Piqueta), near Manacor, Mallorca, Spain. 15 April 2017: speleologist Xisco Gràcia (54 or 55, reported) and buddy Guillem Mascaró were surveying when a guideline broke. Mascaró took the remaining tanks to fetch help while Gràcia waited in an air pocket about 900 m (2,952 ft) from the entrance. An attempt to drill a supply hole failed to reach him. Rescue divers reached him after ~60 hours (one outlet says 48), slowed by murky water. He went back to the cave a month later.
why_potential: A rare survival story in a death-heavy niche. Brand-safe, with built-in clock and hope triggers. Little Shorts coverage was found (open lane). A single chamber plus a single diver makes it very feasible. The ending of rescuers' lights appearing in the water can loop back to frame 1.

working_title: The Greatest Cave Diver Ever Tried to Reach 1,000 ft
alt_title: Sheck Exley's Last Dive
subject: Zacatón, Tamaulipas, Mexico. 6 April 1994: Sheck Exley (45), a pioneer of cave diving and author of its safety rules, died trying to descend past 1,000 ft. Partner Jim Bowden turned back short of gas at about 925 ft (one source) and survived. Exley's body was found wrapped in his descent line when the team pulled up their gear. The cause of death could not be determined.
why_potential: The irony that the man who wrote cave diving's safety rules died in a cave is a strong curiosity gap. It pairs with the Shaw story (Shaw called Exley a hero, reported). A vertical cenote and a depth race are trivial to animate.

working_title: The Swimming Hole With a Trap at the Bottom
alt_title: Jacob's Well: The Diver Who Was Missing for 22 Years
subject: Jacob's Well, Wimberley, Texas, USA. An artesian swimming hole above a cave of four chambers. The death toll is disputed (8–9 to 12+). In the late 1970s Kent Maupin and Mark Brashier died in the narrow fourth chamber, which is prone to gravel slides; a local diver was half-buried in sliding gravel in the third chamber trying to recover them. Maupin's remains were only located in October 2000. The cave is now closed to all diving except the Jacob's Well Exploration Project.
why_potential: FatalBreakdown's Jacob's Well (1.51M) and clickbait copycats ('what their cameras found at the bottom') show steady search demand. Swimmers jumping in above a deadly cave is a perfect contrast shot.

working_title: His Helmet Camera Kept Recording as He Sank
alt_title: The Blue Hole's Arch
subject: Blue Hole, Dahab, Egypt. 28 April 2000: 22-year-old diving instructor Yuri Lipski died after an uncontrolled descent; nitrogen narcosis is suspected. The depth is reported as ~91 m by many outlets and 115 m by Wikipedia's Blue Hole article. His helmet camera was recovered and the footage circulates widely (we will NOT use or trace it). Technical diver Tarek Omar recovered the body the next day. The Blue Hole's 'Arch' at ~55 m has lured many divers; its death toll is disputed.
why_potential: 'World's deadliest dive site' is the topic of Dive Talk's 9.15M outlier. Lipski reaction videos exist (293K). The arch is cavern/overhead rather than a true cave but sits squarely with the cave audience. Ethical treatment is mandatory: focus on the arch trap and narcosis, not on the death footage.

working_title: Divers Found a 12,000-Year-Old Girl in a Flooded Pit
alt_title: The Girl at the Bottom of the Black Hole
subject: Hoyo Negro, Sac Actun system, Quintana Roo, Mexico. 2007: divers Alejandro (Alex) Álvarez, Franco Attolini and Alberto Nava Blank (Archaeology Magazine also lists Danny Riordan) found a ~190-ft-deep pit holding Ice Age animal bones and a near-complete skeleton of a teenage girl, later named 'Naia'. Chatters et al., Science 344 (2014), dated her to ~12,000–13,000 years using tooth enamel, calcite 'florets' and bat guano.
why_potential: A discovery story that is broad-audience, brand-safe and educational. It has a strong reveal (a skull in torchlight, depicted respectfully as stylised remains) and pairs with the 'unexplored underwater' fascination. Less proven demand, but a fresh lane.

working_title: A Hole in a Sheep Paddock That Swallowed Divers
alt_title: The Shaft: Australia's Darkest Dive
subject: The Shaft, a flooded sinkhole on farmland near Mount Gambier, South Australia. 28 May 1973: a group of eight or nine divers (accounts differ) visited; four experienced ocean divers with little cave experience went beyond their planned limits without a guideline, stirred up silt in a tunnel, got lost and drowned. Their bodies were recovered over the following year. The event led to a national reassessment of cave-diving rules. Access is now restricted to CDAA-accredited divers. MrBallen's '16 deaths' claim is unverified.

subject: Tank Cave, near Tantanoola, South Australia (a maze of 7+ km of passages). 27 Feb 2011: explorer, maritime archaeologist and underwater filmmaker Agnes Milowka (29) became separated from her buddy and drowned after running out of air, about 550 m from the entrance at ~20 m depth. working_title: The Deepest Underwater Cave on Earth Has No Bottom (Yet)
alt_title: Hranice Abyss: 400 m and Counting
subject: Hranice Abyss (Hranická propast), Czech Republic. The deepest known flooded cave. On 27 Sep 2016 a team led by Polish diver Krzysztof Starnawski positioned a GRALmarine ROV through a slot at ~200 m; it reached 404 m without finding the bottom. Wikipedia now gives a greatest confirmed depth of 519.5 m, of which ~450 m is underwater. A 2020 geophysics study suggested it might reach ~1 km, a claim later challenged in a rebuttal paper (disputed).
why_potential: 'Bottomless' and 'deepest' superlatives are proven title formulas ('The Horrifying Incidents in This Bottomless Cave'). Pure geology means no victims and low ethics risk. Strong comparison visuals (Eiffel Tower and skyscrapers next to the depth).

working_title: Divers Connected Two Caves and Made the Longest on Earth

subject: Sac Actun, near Tulum, Quintana Roo, Mexico. January 2018: after ~10 months of fieldwork, the Gran Acuífero Maya (GAM) project announced it had found the connection between Sac Actun (~263 km) and Dos Ojos (~83 km), making a single system of ~347 km. That made it the longest known underwater cave, ahead of Ox Bel Ha (~270 km). By naming convention, Dos Ojos became part of Sac Actun.
why_potential: A map-reveal Short where the record and scale are the hook. A cheap 2.5D map animation. Weak story arc and moderate demand. Good for a series about the cenote world.

working_title: They Built a Robot Map of a Cave by Hand
alt_title: Wakulla Springs: Mapping the Dark in 3D
subject: Wakulla Springs, Florida, USA. The US Deep Caving Team expedition led by Bill Stone left on 24 Oct 1987 and ran 70 days with 20 people (including Sheck Exley and Wes Skiles), pushing ~1,270 m (4,160 ft) into the system. In Dec 1987 Stone made a 24-hour dive on his Cis-Lunar MK1 rebreather. The 1998 Wakulla 2 expedition (151 volunteers) produced the first 3D map of an underwater cave using Stone's Digital Wall Mapper.
why_potential: A niche tech story with low demand evidence. It has a visual hook (a laser-scanned cave appearing) that our pipeline can make. Kept as a low-ranked option for variety.
